question.text: Is the Hawkins sign able to predict necrosis in fractures of the neck of the astragalus?
question.context: To assess if the Hawkins sign can predict whether or not astragalus fractures of the neck will develop avascular necrosis. It is also assessed whether the occurrence of this complication is related to the displacement of the fracture, soft tissue injury, or delay in the reduction or surgery. The results were compared with those found in the literature. A retrospective study was conducted on 23 talar neck fractures recorded over a a period of thirteen years. The following variables were analysed: displacement of the fracture, soft tissue injury, delay and type of treatment, complications, observation of the Hawkins sign, and functional outcome. There were 7 type I Hawkins fractures, 11 type II, and 4 type III and 1 type IV. Four cases developed avascular necrosis (2 Hawkins type II and 2 type III). Hawkins sign was observed in 12 cases, of which none developed necrosis. Four cases with negative Hawkins sign developed necrosis. No statistically significant differences were found when comparing the development of avascular necrosis with the displacement of the fracture, soft tissue injury, or delay in treatment. Differences were found when comparing the development of avascular necrosis with the Hawkins sign (P=.03).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a statistically significant association between the presence of the Hawkins sign and the development of avascular necrosis in astragalus neck fractures. This suggests that the Hawkins sign can be a predictor of necrosis.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Differences were found when comparing the development of avascular necrosis with the Hawkins sign (P=.03).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While displacement, soft tissue injury, and delay in treatment were not significantly associated with necrosis, the Hawkins sign was. This suggests the Hawkins sign is a more specific indicator of necrosis in this context.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a statistically significant association (P=.03) between Hawkins sign and development of avascular necrosis, with 4 necrosis cases in the negative Hawkins group versus none in the positive group. While this suggests the sign may be predictive, the small sample size (only 1 case with Hawkins type IV) and the fact that no other variables showed significant differences limit definitive conclusions. The moderate p-value indicates a trend but not strong evidence.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The statistically significant association (P=.03) between Hawkins sign and necrosis development
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Other variables like displacement, soft tissue injury, and delay in treatment did not show significant differences, making Hawkins sign the most relevant predictor identified in this study

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found a statistically significant difference (P=.03) between the presence of the Hawkins sign and the development of avascular necrosis, with no necrosis observed in cases with a positive Hawkins sign, while 4 cases with a negative Hawkins sign developed necrosis. This suggests the Hawkins sign is predictive of necrosis avoidance.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: P=.03 significance level showing association between Hawkins sign and absence of necrosis
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Displacement, soft tissue injury, and delay in treatment were ruled out as predictors due to lack of statistical significance, making Hawkins sign the only significant predictor.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other factors such as fracture displacement, soft tissue injury, and treatment delay were not statistically linked to avascular necrosis in this study, but these variables were not thoroughly assessed. The lack of a perfect predictive relationship means the Hawkins sign alone is insufficient to determine necrosis risk.
